summary: Adds an Intermediate Exchange to IKEv2, the key-setup protocol used by IPsec, so that large amounts of data can be sent while the security association is being established. A key motivation is key exchange methods that resist quantum computers, which often have very large public values that do not fit well in the initial messages. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: When two computers set up a secret handshake, the first messages are small. This adds a middle step so they can pass bigger notes, like very large secret codes, before finishing the handshake.

questions: how does ikev2 send large key exchange data
what is the ikev2 intermediate exchange
how to use post-quantum keys with ikev2
subtitle: A new IKEv2 exchange that lets peers move large amounts of data, such as post-quantum public keys, before authentication.

tldr.problem: IKE fragmentation cannot be used in the first IKEv2 exchange (IKE_SA_INIT), so large data, such as the big public keys of quantum-resistant key exchange methods, would cause IP fragmentation.
tldr.mechanism: One or more IKE_INTERMEDIATE exchanges (Exchange Type 43) run between IKE_SA_INIT and IKE_AUTH, are protected by the Encrypted payload, can use IKE fragmentation, and are authenticated later via an IntAuth value added to the AUTH calculation.
tldr.outcome: Peers can transfer tens of kilobytes before the IKE SA is established without IP fragmentation, but the data is not authenticated until IKE_AUTH completes, so specifications must cap the number of exchanges.

facts.label: Expected data volume
facts.value: Tens of kilobytes in most cases

today: RFC 9242 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It leaves the specific uses, such as which data to carry, to separate specifications.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
IKEv2 (RFC 7296) uses UDP. If a message is bigger than the Path MTU (PMTU), IP fragmentation happens, which causes operational problems in some networks. RFC 7383 defines IKE fragmentation to avoid this, but it cannot be used in the initial IKE_SA_INIT exchange. That was not a problem while IKE_SA_INIT messages were small.

Quantum-computer (QC) resistant key exchange methods usually have large public keys, so sending them in IKE_SA_INIT would probably cause IP fragmentation. Using TCP as in RFC 8229 is a last resort with significant drawbacks. So this RFC adds the Intermediate Exchange, written IKE_INTERMEDIATE, which may occur one or more times right after IKE_SA_INIT and before IKE_AUTH.

The exchange is defined without tying it to one use case. It is not meant for bulk transfer, and the RFC expects tens of kilobytes in most cases (a few hundred kilobytes in extreme cases). It should be used only for data needed to establish the IKE SA.
sections.eli5: The first hello is a tiny envelope that cannot hold a big gift. This adds a middle step with room to send bigger things, in smaller pieces.

sections.title: Negotiating Support
sections.content:
The initiator signals support by including a notification of type INTERMEDIATE_EXCHANGE_SUPPORTED in its IKE_SA_INIT request. If the responder supports the exchange, it includes the same notification in its response.

It is a Status Type notification with Notify Message Type 16438. Protocol ID and SPI Size are both 0, and the notification data is empty. Implementations MUST ignore non-empty data if they do not understand its purpose.
sections.eli5: Each side raises a hand to say "I can do the middle step too." Only if both hands go up does it happen.

sections.title: Running the Exchange
sections.content:
If both peers indicated support, the initiator may use one or more IKE_INTERMEDIATE exchanges (Exchange Type 43). Using them is optional. Because the window size starts at 1, the exchanges MUST be sequential and MUST all finish before IKE_AUTH starts. The IKE SA MUST NOT be considered established until IKE_AUTH succeeds.

Message IDs follow the standard IKEv2 rule: 1 for the first IKE_INTERMEDIATE exchange, 2 for the next, and so on. Implementations MUST verify this. The first IKE_AUTH messages use the next value after the last intermediate exchange. If NAT is detected in IKE_SA_INIT, peers switch to port 4500 in the first IKE_INTERMEDIATE exchange.

The Encrypted payload MUST be present in these messages, and payloads with large data MUST be placed inside it, so IKE fragmentation can apply if both peers negotiated it. The message contents are left to the specifications that use the exchange.
sections.eli5: The two sides take turns, one note at a time, and finish all the middle notes before the real introductions begin.

sections.title: Protecting the Messages
sections.content: Keys SK_e and SK_a for IKE_INTERMEDIATE exchanges are computed in the standard way from RFC 7296. Each exchange uses the most recently calculated keys. The first uses those from IKE_SA_INIT. If an exchange performs an additional key exchange and updates the keys, the next one uses the updated keys; otherwise the old keys are reused. After the last intermediate exchange, the latest keys protect IKE_AUTH and everything after it.
sections.eli5: Everyone keeps using the latest secret code. If a new code is agreed in one step, the next step uses it.

sections.title: Authenticating the Exchanges
sections.content:
IKE_INTERMEDIATE messages are authenticated in IKE_AUTH by adding their content to the AUTH payload calculation. The on-the-wire form cannot be used, because IKE fragmentation lets a sender resend a message in a different form (for example fragmented, or with different fragment sizes), and implementations do not know which form the peer got. So the content is taken before encryption and fragmentation.

A new chunk, IntAuth, is appended to the signed or MACed octets. It consists of IntAuth_iN, IntAuth_rN and IKE_AUTH_MID, the Message ID of the first IKE_AUTH round as a four-octet integer in network byte order. Each IntAuth_[i/r]n is the negotiated PRF applied to the previous value joined with the content of this exchange's request or response.

That content has two chunks: A, from the first octet of the IKE Header to the last octet of the Encrypted payload's generic header, and optionally P, the plaintext inner payloads. The Length fields are adjusted so they do not count the IV, padding, pad length and checksum fields. The PRF MUST be applied to whole messages before fragmentation, and fragmented messages MUST be reassembled first. Each calculation uses the latest SK_p keys from before that exchange started.
sections.eli5: To prove the middle notes were not tampered with, both sides keep a running fingerprint of what was said and check it at the end.

sections.title: Errors and Other Extensions
sections.content:
Messages are not authenticated until IKE_AUTH completes, so errors must be handled carefully, trading better diagnostics against the risk of helping a DoS attack. The error handling for initial IKEv2 exchanges in RFC 7296 also applies, though not every error notification can appear (authentication errors, for instance, apply only to IKE_AUTH).

IKE_INTERMEDIATE MAY be used in IKEv2 Session Resumption (RFC 5723) between IKE_SESSION_RESUME and IKE_AUTH. Peers MUST negotiate it again by including the notification in the IKE_SESSION_RESUME messages, since support is not stored in the resumption ticket.
sections.eli5: Since nobody has proved who they are yet, the helpers are careful about what they say when something goes wrong.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Data in IKE_INTERMEDIATE exchanges is not authenticated until IKE_AUTH completes. If it is inside the Encrypted payload, it is protected from passive eavesdroppers, and a valid Integrity Checksum Data shows the message came from the party that did IKE_SA_INIT.

Because authentication happens only in IKE_AUTH, a malicious initiator could run many intermediate exchanges, send a lot of data and then abort. Specifications using the exchange MUST NOT allow an unlimited number of exchanges at the initiator's discretion. The responder should know the exact number, or a hard maximum must be set. RFC 8019 gives guidance on DoS during IKE SA establishment.

If an attacker could break the key exchange in real time, for example with a quantum computer, the attacker could read and forge the data. The forgery would show up in IKE_AUTH, but forged messages could still enable a DoS. If the negotiated PRF is not secure against a second preimage attack with known key, forgery might go undetected.
sections.eli5: Strangers could keep sending huge letters just to waste your time, so the rules limit how many middle steps are allowed.
